Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verses 70–73:

Now the address turns to a subject closer to the human self than the animals, trees, fruits, honeybees and the blessings of honey: a subject connected with the depths of human personality. The various stages of human life, a person's lifespan, his sustenance, his spouse, and his children and grandchildren are among the most particular topics of human interest. Man is greatly moved by such matters, because they are the fields of his activities and concerns.

Verses 70 to 73

The first of these sensitive subjects concerns human life, human death and the stages of life, and it is a beloved topic of interest for all people. By reflecting on human life, certainly, even the hardest-hearted person sometimes feels tenderness, and he begins to think that all the blessings bestowed upon him are in the hand of Allah alone. When the thought of the loss of these blessings is placed in a person's heart, there can arise within him the sense of God-fearing that is deposited in his innate nature, the intuition of taqwa (God-consciousness), and an inclination towards the Giver of this life. Especially in the circumstances of old age, when a person enters *ardhal al-'umr* (the most abject old age), he begins to forget knowledge and once again becomes simple, helpless and unaware, like a child. When a person reflects seriously on such circumstances, and considers his present youth, strength, knowledge, honour and dignity, he can, to a considerable extent, come onto the right path.

*Inna Allaha 'alimun qadir* (16:70): "Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." This conclusion is mentioned here so that man should acknowledge the reality that complete, eternal and everlasting knowledge belongs to Allah alone, and true, eternal and everlasting power is also with Allah alone. Man's knowledge is also limited and subject to decline, and man's power is also limited and subject to decline; even in his knowledge and power there is only partial knowledge and partial power.

In these verses, the second point concerns the means of human sustenance. In the field of sustenance, the difference between one individual and another has also been taken into account. The Holy Qur'an explicitly states that there is a difference among people regarding sustenance, that Allah has given some preference over others, and that this preference too is subject to the Sunnah of Allah. This disparity in ranks is not merely accidental; rather, the profound wisdom of Allah is hidden within it as well. Sometimes it happens that a person is a great scholar, thinker and intelligent, yet his means of sustenance and his capacity for progress in it are limited, because Allah has given such people precious abilities in other fields.

In contrast, another person will appear very simple, rebellious and jahili (ignorant of the truth), yet he will be very skilful in the field of acquiring sustenance and its growth. Furthermore, there is diversity and variation in abilities among people. Sometimes people do not reflect and assume that sustenance has no connection with abilities, whereas the acquisition of sustenance is itself one of the abilities. Moreover, sometimes an abundance of sustenance is a trial from Allah, while even in scarcity of sustenance there is sometimes some hidden wisdom, and on the basis of that wisdom Allah tests certain people. In any case, the difference in sustenance and means of sustenance is a reality that exists, and its basis is the difference in abilities. However, the variation in sustenance will be in accordance with abilities only when, in society, there is no oppressive control over the opportunities for acquiring sustenance and no artificial disparity, as is the case in the corrupt societies of today. This verse points to the society that existed at the time of the Messenger ﷺ in the Age of Ignorance. By presenting this situation as an example, Allah corrects one belief within the system of polytheistic ideas. In the idolatrous society of Makkah it was customary, as we have already explained, that these people would dedicate some of the wealth given by Allah to their idols. Allah says: Look, you also have slaves, just as you are slaves of Allah (it should be remembered that the institution of slavery existed in the Jahili society of that time). You certainly do not like these slaves to become equal partners with you in your earnings; so how would Allah approve that some of His creations and possessions should become the property of those who have been wrongly made partners in the divine affairs of Allah?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verse 76:

Verses 75 to 76

The first example is drawn from the actual situation that existed among them. In the pagan society of Arabia at that time there were owned slaves (mamlukah ghulam). They were such a helpless creation that they owned nothing and had no authority over anything. These people were also well aware of the difference in rank between the master who has full power and disposal, and the helpless slave who has no authority. Therefore they were told: how can you equate the True Master with your slaves, and make these slaves partners of the Master? For all human beings are slaves and servants of Allah.

The second example is of a man who is mute, incapable (balid), ... and a burden. He knows nothing of any task; he is a burden on his master. Wherever he is sent, he cannot accomplish any good deed. But the other person is strong of body, sound of mind, speaks well, speaks in justice and fairness, and is upright in conduct, standing on the straight path. No sound-minded person can establish equality between these two individuals. Then how can partnership and equality be established between an idol, a stone, and Allah, the All-Powerful and All-Knowing, when Allah commands that you enjoin what is good (ma'ruf), forbid the people from what is evil (munkar), and come to the straight path?

This lesson, which began with Allah's command not to hold the view of two equal masters (jadd al-yayn), concluded with these two examples, through which it was established that polytheistic beliefs and doctrines are astonishing.

The question of resurrection after death is a matter that has been extremely disputed in every age. People have engaged in dialogue, dispute and debate with every messenger over it. In its essence, it is that unseen matter which is among the most particular secrets of Allah.

Tashreeh:

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ (16:77). The knowledge of the hidden realities of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone. The condition of human beings is that they are incapable and powerless to uncover the secrets and mysteries concealed behind the veil of the unseen. However far their material knowledge advances, and however many treasures of knowledge about the material things of the world are opened to them, and however large a quantity of the hidden treasures within the earth they may discover, they cannot attain these secrets of the universe. Whereas even the chosen human being, who knows the most about the unseen matters in this universe, does not know what is going to happen to his own self tomorrow; rather, he does not even know whether the breath he exhales will return or not. The world of human desires is vast and wide, but from behind the veil of the unseen, destiny laughs at him. He does not know what is going to happen to him in the next moment. Sometimes, in the very next moment, he has to face difficulties. It is a great mercy of Allah that He has kept human beings unaware of the events that will come in the next moment, so that they remain hopeful at all times, keep working, keep creating and keep nurturing, and leave behind the works they have begun so that those who come after will complete them, until destiny brings forth the face that lies behind the veil.

The Hour too is among these hidden and concealed unseen matters. If people were to know the exact time of the establishment of the Hour, the wheel of life would either stop suddenly or suffer a great disruption. The days and nights of life would not pass in the manner that the law of nature has organized for them; rather, people would sit down and count the years, months, days and hours, saying: now only so many days of the Hour remain.

﴿And the matter of the Hour is not but as a glance of the eye or even nearer﴾ (16:77). The establishment of the Hour will not take any longer than the blink of an eye, or even less than that. It is very near, yet the reckoning of its time differs from the reckoning of years and months of human beings, with different measures. Allah does not need any time for its arrangements. The blink of an eye is sufficient; in even less time than that, it will appear before you with all its scenes.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ (16:77). The truth is that Allah is capable of all things. Bringing together this countless number of human beings and creatures, raising them, gathering them, taking account, and giving reward and punishment is not difficult for that power which need only say "Be," and it is. This matter is frightening and difficult only for those who think about affairs by human measures, look at them with human eyes, and calculate them in human numbers. Therefore their thinking and estimates go wrong.

Allah, the Exalted, makes this great event comprehensible to human beings through some examples from human life, because the power of human perception and the power of imagination are incapable of a true conception of this great and terrifying event. These examples are repeated within human life.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verse 78:

Verse: "And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing..." to "...that you may be grateful." (87)

Explanation:

This too is one of the unseen realities (ʿalam-e-ghayb), which is very close to human beings and yet, despite its closeness, is far beyond comprehension and understanding: how the foetus (janin) in the womb passes through the stages of its completion. Sometimes people observe the conditions of the foetus, but their knowledge is limited, and they cannot determine how it passes through the stages of completion and growth, because the secret of life in its development is the real secret, the mystery of which remains hidden to this day. The knowledge that man claims, and with which he advances, and through which he seeks to discover even the establishment of the Hour, is a knowledge that is newly acquired (ḥādith), because previously man knew nothing at all.

"And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing at all" (16:78). The birth of every scholar and every researcher, and their emerging from their mother's womb in a state in which they know nothing, is an event that is near at hand. Thereafter, the knowledge that they learn is the religion of Allah, and this is what Allah has given to man only to the extent sufficient for living in this world, that is, in this entire universe spread around man.

"And He made for you hearing, sight and hearts" (16:78). The Qur'an applies the word qalb (heart) and fu'ad to the totality of human faculties of perception. It includes reason, and it includes those intuitive and inspired powers whose reality man is not aware of. And man also does not know how these powers operate; and He gave you hearing, sight and hearts.

"That perhaps you may be grateful" (16:78). When you reflect on how great the favour of Allah is in giving these things to man, and, in addition, when you obtain Allah's other blessings through these faculties of perception, you should thank Allah; and the first manifestation of gratitude is that a person believes in Allah alone.

Another wondrous scene, which is among the signs of divine mercy and which is commonplace among people, is that a person sees it and does not reflect upon it.

The birds are made subservient within the expanse of the sky and earth. They fly about in it, right before our eyes. We see this sight again and again, and because we see it repeatedly, the wonder within it has become imperceptible. The human heart and mind turn their attention to it only when a person is awake and has been given a poetic power of observation. A person with a poetic vision can write a poem and an ode on it, and spontaneously, on beholding this ancient, familiar and yet fresh poetic scene, can say:

﴿يُمْسِكُهُنَّ إِلَّا اللَّهُ﴾ (16:79) "Who holds them up but Allah?"

How this happens: the very nature of birds was fashioned upon such principles, and Allah made the atmospheric conditions around them such that they can fly in it and never fall to the ground at any moment.

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ لِّقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (16:79) "Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verse 81:

Now the theme advances a step further, as it describes the secrets and wonders of Allah's creation. Further signs of Allah's power and further examples of His blessings are presented: people's homes and their joys, the atmosphere of the home, its furnishings, and shelters.

Those who understand how great a blessing a home is, and how peaceful a home is, are those who have become emigrants, who have been driven out of their homes and wander from place to place. They have neither a home nor tranquility. Here, the mention of homes and shades follows the mention of the unseen (ghayb). The connection is that a shade also covers something, and the unseen also covers the matters that are hidden within it. In both there is concealment and privacy. Only a sensitive person can fully enjoy the description of homes as a place of tranquility; heedless people cannot enjoy it as they should. It is appropriate here to explain what Islam's view of the home is. The Qur'an describes the home in this way:

﴿And Allah has made for you, from your homes, a place of rest﴾ (16:80). Islam wants a home to be a place of psychological comfort, mental stability and emotional peace. It should be a place of joy, where people come and are happy. And within it there should be provision for a person's material and spiritual tranquility. Those who live in it should be a source of reassurance and joy for one another, and each one should be a means of tranquility for the others. Islam does not want any home to become a place of dispute, quarrels, discord and enmity, because in its view a home should be a place of settling, peace, security, and well-being and safety.

This is why Islam guarantees the sanctity of the home, so that the peace, tranquility and safety of the home can be guaranteed. For example, no person is permitted to enter another's home without permission. No one is permitted to simply barge into another's home without right and without permission. Likewise, no one is permitted, for any reason, to interfere in the privacy of others without the permission of the household. Nor is anyone permitted to spy on a home, nor to backbite about anyone, because by these matters the peace, tranquility, joy and contentment of any home can be destroyed. That is why the Qur'an has described the home as a place of tranquility.

Since this scene concerned the home, shelter and clothing, the aspect of animals that is useful for these purposes is also mentioned here, namely the aspect of dwelling and clothing.

﴿And He made for you, from the skins of livestock, dwellings which you find light on the day you travel and the day you stay; and from their wool, their fur and their hair, furnishings and provisions for a time﴾ (16:80). Here too, the needs among the benefits of animals are mentioned, and also mentioned are the things that bring beauty and pleasure. This is the difference between mata' (provision, enjoyment) and athath (furnishings, household goods). Mata' refers to carpets, rugs and other decorative items, but it includes everything that falls under the description of enjoyment and brings delight.

In an atmosphere of peace and tranquility, the mode of expression now becomes gentle. The discussion turns to shades, shelters, mountains, heat and cold, and battle garments.

﴿And Allah has made for you, of what He has created, shades; and He has made for you shelters in the mountains; and He has made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you in your fighting﴾ (16:81). Within the shade there is tranquility for a person, and even the very idea of shade brings delight. In mountain shelters a person feels comfort and security. Then the garments that serve in cold, in heat, and in the state of war are a source of human interest and essential for a person's protection. Moreover, there is joy and happiness in them, and so the following conclusion emerges from this.

Lesson No. 321: At a Glance

The previous lesson ended on this verse:

﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things, and as guidance, mercy and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ (16:89) "And O Prophet, We have sent down to you this Book in which there is an explanation of everything, and guidance, mercy and good news for the Muslims." Accordingly, this lesson explains some of its teachings, that is, what the teachings are that are guidance, mercy and good tidings. That it contains justice, benevolence, the command to spend on relatives, the prohibition of immorality, the prohibition of sin and transgression, and also the command to fulfill promises and the prohibition of breaking oaths. These are the important and fundamental teachings that this Book emphasizes.

In this lesson, breaking a covenant is declared a crime; likewise, misleading people by swearing oaths and deceiving them is declared a great crime, and for it there is a severe warning of a great punishment. In contrast, for those who are patient there is good news that they will be rewarded for their good deeds.

After this, the etiquette of reciting the Great Book is explained, such as seeking refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan before recitation, so that this rejected one flees from the gathering of the recitation of the Qur'an. Also mentioned are some fabricated statements of the polytheists about the Great Book. For example, some polytheists used to say that, God forbid, the Prophet (ﷺ) himself fabricates words and wrongly attributes them to God. Some used to say that there is a non-Arab slave who tells these things to the Prophet (ﷺ).

At the end of this lesson, mention is made of the punishment of those who, after believing, adopt disbelief. Also mentioned are those who are compelled to disbelief while their hearts remain content with faith. And mention is made of the chosen people who were persecuted because of their faith, and who migrated, struggled, and were patient. All these matters are clear guidance from Allah, the best direction, a mercy from Allah, and good tidings for the people of faith.

The main purpose of the revelation of the Quran, according to this doctrine, is to bring a nation into the field of action, to form a society that acts upon these teachings. A new world is to be created and a new system established. A universal call and movement is to be raised which is not partisan to any group, tribe or race. In this call, the basis of collective relationship and connection shall not be any tribalism (asabiyyah) or nationalism.

Accordingly, the teachings of this Book are based on those principles upon which a society and an ummah can be formed. On these teachings and principles, individuals, nations and peoples should have full satisfaction, and in their mutual dealings, relations, promises and agreements there should be full trust.

The first teaching of this Book relates to justice ('adl). A just system in which the rights of an individual, a group, a nation and all nations are protected. This justice should not be influenced by anyone's desire, nor by love or hatred. There should be no trace of kinship or nepotism in it. It should be equal for the rich and the poor; the rights of the strong and the weak should be equal in it. This justice should walk straight on its path, and in it there should be one standard and one measure for all.

Along with this justice, the teachings of this Book are based on another important principle, ihsan (excellence and benevolence). As far as justice is concerned, its sword is extremely sharp, strong and unbending, and it cuts straight through. But Islamic teachings, along with justice, have also kept open the door of ihsan to win hearts. It is not obligatory that one must always take one's rights in accordance with unbending justice; if someone wishes to forgo his rights, this is better for him. Through this, the enmity of hearts is removed and wounds are healed. Moreover, it manifests the virtues of character and noble conduct.

The concept of ihsan is very broad. Every good deed is ihsan. Every action and every dealing comes under the command of ihsan: a person's relationship with his Lord, a person's relationship with his family, a person's relationship with the community, and a person's relationship with all of humanity.

Some commentators, merely because this verse is Meccan, have taken justice to refer to obligatory worship ('ibadat wajibiyyah) and ihsan to refer to voluntary worship ('ibadat nafliyyah), because Islamic laws had not been revealed in Makkah. But justice and ihsan include, besides law, moral dealings and individual conduct as well, so it is not correct to restrict them to acts of worship.

One form of ihsan is maintaining ties of kinship (silat al-rahm) and spending on relatives, and the specific command for it has been given because in Islam it has very great importance and dignity and very strong emphasis. The basic thinking behind it is not tribal partisanship of the family, but its purpose and aim is the family system and the Islamic system of collective social security (takaful ijtima'i) built upon the family system. Islam has made the family the first unit of its collective system and then gradually extends it to society, because Islam has its own view regarding collective social security (Security).

"And He forbids immorality, wrongdoing and oppression (al-baghy)" (16:90). Fahsha' refers to everything that exceeds its limit. It is mostly used for transgression that is against a person's private honour, because sexual licentiousness is also an act carried out beyond its bounds. In it too there is excess and transgression of limits. Generally, this word has become specific to sexual licentiousness. Al-munkar is that act which sound human nature (fitrah salimah) denies, and Shariah also regards it as munkar for this very reason, because the Islamic Shariah and the Islamic system are a natural system. Shariah and law remain established in their place, while human nature sometimes becomes corrupted. At the time of corruption of nature, then Shariah becomes the standard. Al-baghy means oppression and encroachment upon people's rights.

No society in the world can remain established on immorality, munkarat and oppression. A society in which immorality is widespread can never remain established, and likewise a society in which munkarat have made people their captives can never flourish. No national system can remain standing whose foundation is oppression.

No society tolerates such a collective system for very long; soon people begin to protest against that system, even if such an oppressive and tyrannical system is powerful and majestic. Even if those in authority in such a collective system use unlimited resources to support and preserve that system. If human history is studied in detail, this history is in reality made up of continuous protest against immorality, munkarat and oppression. Therefore, it does not matter that for some period in history some collective system remained founded upon immorality, munkarat and oppression; the lesson history gives is this, because against such systems there has always been protest and reaction. In such systems, they have been a foreign body to the body of the Islamic society, and human society has always thrown such systems off and cast them away, just as every body reacts against the entry of a foreign body within itself. Therefore, Allah's command to enjoin justice and ihsan and to forbid immorality, munkarat and oppression is in exact accordance with sound human nature. Islam, by declaring this natural reaction an Islamic struggle (jihad), gives it strength. This is why the commentary on this command comes in this instructive form:

"He admonishes you that you may take heed" (16:90). This admonition is so that you may return to your original nature and remember it.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verse 91:

﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have made it, and do not break your oaths after their confirmation, although you have made Allah your surety. Indeed, Allah knows what you do.﴾ (16:91)

The covenant of Allah includes the pledge made by the Muslims to the Prophet ﷺ, and it also includes the covenants that Allah has commanded. Moreover, the establishment of relations in any human society rests solely on people respecting their covenants. Without this, no society can survive at all, and humanity itself cannot endure. This verse rebukes people who, after firmly binding themselves by a covenant, break it, even though they have made Allah the witness and guarantor of that covenant, and the covenant was made in the name of Allah. It is a warning, though not a light one.

﴿Indeed, Allah knows what you do.﴾

Islam has been very strict regarding the fulfilment of covenants. It does not permit overlooking this at any time, because the fulfilment of covenants is the foundation on which the entire collective order stands, and without it the collective order collapses. The Islamic texts, the Qur'an and the Sunnah, have not been satisfied merely with commanding the fulfilment of covenants and issuing a threat against breaking them. Rather, they have repeatedly emphasised it, explained the evils of breaking a covenant, and sought to remove all the causes and circumstances that might at any time lead to the breaking of a covenant.

The Qur'an says:

﴿And do not be like the woman who untwists her thread, after it has been made strong, into pieces. You take your oaths as a means of deception between yourselves, so that one community may become more prosperous than another. Allah only tests you through this. And on the Day of Resurrection He will surely make clear to you that about which you used to differ.﴾ (61 : 19)

"Your condition should not become like that of the woman who spun her thread herself and then herself tore it into pieces. You make your oaths a weapon of deceit in your mutual dealings, so that one people may gain more than another. Yet Allah tests you through this covenant, and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection the truth of all your disputes."

Whoever breaks a covenant is like that foolish woman who is weak and who constantly changes her decision and resolve. She keeps spinning thread, then breaks it, and having torn it into pieces, she makes it into thread again. Every element of this parable expresses wonder and contempt, and makes the woman's act a shameful and detestable deed. This is the real purpose of the comparison. No person of noble character would wish to become like this weak-willed, foolish woman who does something from which she gains nothing.

Some of those people were considering breaking the covenant they had made with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the grounds that the following of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was small and that he was weak, while the following of Quraysh was large by comparison. Therefore such people were warned that it is no justification for them to make such sworn agreements a means of deception and faithlessness, and to cast them off from their necks at any time.

﴿Do not make your oaths a means of deception between yourselves, lest one community be greater than another.﴾ (61 : 29) That is, do not make your oaths a weapon of deceit in your mutual dealings, because one community is greater than another. In other words, because one people is greater in number than another, and your interest is tied to the community with the larger numbers.

The meaning of this verse also includes that a person should not break a covenant merely because the interests of some state demand it. For example, a government first makes an agreement with another government, or with a group of governments, and then breaks it merely because there is a larger bloc of nations elsewhere, and that government's interests are tied to that other bloc. Islam does not take such interests into consideration. Islam requires that a covenant be fulfilled in every situation, and that no covenant be used as a means of deception or of gaining advantage. This condition is in addition to the requirement that any covenant be founded only upon righteousness and the fear of God. No covenant should be made at all for objectionable purposes or purposes that disobey God. No covenant should be made on the basis of sin, wickedness, and disobedience. It is inconceivable that a covenant should be made in order to plunder nations and peoples. This is the principle upon which the Islamic community (jama'ah) was formed, and this has always been the policy of the Islamic state. As a result, the whole world was enriched with the wealth of tranquillity, trust, and purity. Muslims continued to deal with individuals and nations on this basis for as long as Muslims were the leaders of the world.

This verse of the Holy Qur'an warns Muslims not to make such considerations a justification for setting aside agreements, and not to allow circumstances to arise in which any person or government is compelled to break a covenant.

﴿Because one community is greater than another.﴾ (61 : 29) This is a trial and a test from Allah. In this way Allah tests their willpower, their loyalty to covenants, and their self-respect, through their respect for the One in whose name they made the covenant. That is, they made Allah a witness over it.

﴿Indeed, Allah is testing you in this matter.﴾ (61 : 29) The disputes that arise between individuals and nations are not finally decided here. Allah says that the final judgment will be made by Allah on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ.﴾ (61 : 29) These words have been brought here as an introduction, as a preface to the matter that even if there is a covenant with people who hold different opinions, ideas, and beliefs, it must be fulfilled. Thus: ﴿If Allah had willed, He would have made you one community, but He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.﴾ (61 : 29)

If Allah had willed, He would have created people with one single capacity. But Allah gave them entirely different abilities, and did not make them copies from one printing plate. He created them in different patterns. Then He set out for them the rules for attaining guidance and for falling into misguidance, and made each person accountable for his own deeds. Therefore, difference of beliefs and religions is not a justification for breaking a covenant. Differences of religion have other causes, which relate to the will of Allah. As for the covenant, it must be fulfilled, even if there is a difference of beliefs. This is the first principle of Islam regarding international dealings and religious tolerance. Islam stands at its peak in this principle, and under the guidance of the Holy Qur'an, this principle was put into practice in this world by Muslims alone.

Further details are given in which the fulfilment of covenants is emphasised, and it is further prohibited that you use a covenant for deception and mischief. This worldly self-interest and the temporary advantages of this lowly world cannot give you that wealth of tranquillity. As a result, all the principles of human psychological and social life will collapse, and a great upheaval will arise in collective affairs and relationships. That was the punishment of this world. As for the Hereafter, such people will face a severe punishment there. Here it is also explained that if you fulfil a covenant and, as a result, suffer some worldly loss, then Allah will also give its reward. The benefits of this world are bound to perish, and the benefits of the Hereafter remain. The treasures of Allah are vast, and with Him is a wealth that never ends.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 16, verse 94:

Commentary: When oaths are used for deception and fraud, the faith dies in the human conscience and its image is distorted in the consciences of others. A person who swears an oath while knowing that he is lying cannot keep any belief settled in his heart. Nor can such a person walk steadfastly on any path. Along with this, he distorts the image of his religion and faith in the eyes of those against whom he swears. The other party comes to know that his oaths were for deception. Thus this person, by repelling those people from the religion of Islam, becomes a cause of their misguidance, because he sets a bad example for other Muslims and for non-Muslims.

When people saw that the people of Islam were very firm in their promises, bound by their covenants, clear in their dealings, and sincere in their faith, then nations and groups entered Islam in large numbers, because the gain from fidelity to covenant and fulfilment of agreements was far greater than the loss they suffered from it.

The Qur'an and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in building the character of Muslims, left very excellent impressions on their lives in this respect, and according to these impressions Muslims dealt with people, both individually and at the level of government. Their conduct was extremely distinctive. It is narrated in the traditions that there was a fixed period of the peace treaty between Mu'awiyah (may Allah be pleased with him) and the Emperor of Rome. Mu'awiyah launched an army against the ruler of Syria before the period of the treaty ended, while the other side did not even know of it. On this occasion, Amr ibn Abasah said: "Allahu Akbar! O Mu'awiyah, fulfil your promise, do not commit treachery. I myself heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever has a term of peace fixed between himself and a people, let him not untie the knot of that covenant until the term has passed.'" So Mu'awiyah returned with his army. Islamic history is full of such narrations, in which Muslims kept their covenants despite the clear benefit of breaking them, and set aside apparent expediency.

The Qur'an had imbued the hearts of Muslims with exactly this Islamic colour. The Qur'an encouraged fidelity to covenants and warned against breaking them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) warned people and declared that the parties to a covenant are not only the two sides, but Allah is also a party. The Qur'an declared that the gain from breaking a covenant is extremely trivial and worthless, and that the reward and recompense Allah gives for fidelity to a covenant will be a very great reward.

﴿And do not sell the covenant of Allah for a small price. Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ (16:95) [The Urdu text cites this as (61:59), but the verse quoted is Surah An-Nahl 16:95.]

Then the Qur'an reminds that whatever people possess, even if it is their own property, is perishable, while what is with Allah is lasting.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 16, verse 96:

﻿"What you have will come to an end, but what Allah has will endure" (16:96). The Qur'an strengthens people's resolve to keep their covenants, encourages them to bear hardships in the path of fulfilling covenants, and promises a good reward to those who are patient through these hardships.

"And We will surely reward those who are patient with their reward according to the best of what they used to do" (16:96). And in this connection, whatever mistakes proceeded from them, We will forgive them. Therefore, in the recompense, only the good aspect of their deeds will be taken into account.

In relation to deeds and recompense, the general principle is stated here.

(1) In regard to reward and punishment, both sexes of mankind, male and female, have the same ruling. In this matter they are completely equal, and their reward and punishment are alike. With Allah there is no distinction between them. Although the word (man) is used for both men and women, the phrase ﴿male or female﴾ (61:79) has been added for emphasis and clarification. In this surah the word is brought in specifically because it also refutes the evil notions of the people of ignorance (Jahiliyyah) about women. For example, the opinion of that society about women was not good, and when a man received news that a daughter had been born to him, his face would darken and he would hide from people, afflicted with distress, shame and disgrace.

Faith is a firm foundation for any moral structure; without it no structure can be built. Without it, deeds will be like a heap of sand which, when a strong storm takes it, is scattered into the air. Belief and ideology are that to which the threads of actions are attached. If this is absent, the warp and woof of actions are torn into pieces and scattered. Belief causes righteous deeds and gives them purpose. Belief and ideology give good deeds a foundation upon which everything else rests and is firm. They do not have impermanence or instability, nor do they keep changing according to interests and desires.

The Qur'an says that if righteous deeds are built on the foundation of faith, the result will be that such people will be granted a good life (hayat tayyibah) in this world as well. It is not necessary that this life be one of luxury, prosperity and wealth; sometimes a believer will have these things, and sometimes he will not. But remember that sometimes a person's life passes very beautifully even with sufficient wealth, provided that the connection with Allah is established, inner peace is attained, and there is reliance upon Allah and the pleasure of Allah is obtained. A person is granted physical health, his desires are balanced, and there is blessing in everything he has. The home environment is good, and there is love in the hearts of the family members. The environment is such that righteous deeds are taking place in it, and because of these deeds there is tranquility in life all around and peace in the conscience. Wealth is only a minor element of peace and tranquility. It is also necessary that wealth be sufficient for one's needs, otherwise it becomes a calamity. But this station is attained by those whose hearts are pure, chosen, and attached to lofty aims that are precious in the sight of Allah.

Remember that the good life of this world does not diminish the reward of the Hereafter. The reward of the Hereafter will be for the good deeds which the people of faith performed, and from ﴿according to the best of what they used to do﴾ (61:79) it is implicitly derived that evil deeds will be disregarded. How good is this treatment, and how abundant is the generosity of the Divine Being.

Seek refuge with Allah from Satan.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verse 99:

﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ (16:99)

Therefore, those who turn wholly to Allah, their hearts become sincere for Allah. Satan cannot overpower them, even though he casts his snares before them, because their connection is with God, and Allah protects them from the snare of that accursed one. They walk alongside Allah and follow behind Allah. It is true that errors sometimes occur from them, but they do not lay down their arms before Satan. Therefore, they keep driving Satan away through seeking refuge (ta'awwudh) and keep returning to Allah.

Now, the claims of the polytheists (mushrikin) concerning the Qur'an, and the response to them.

The polytheists do not know what the function of this Book is. The truth is that this Book has been revealed so that it may bring into existence a global society, namely the Muslim Ummah, and they are unaware of this fact. This Ummah is meant to lead the whole world, and it is the final Ummah. In the future, everything in the world is to be done by it; no new messenger will come down from the heavens now.

Furthermore, Allah, who created man, alone knows what is in man's interest and need. When the purpose of a command is fulfilled and the term of that temporary command is complete, Allah brings a new command, because in new circumstances there is a need for that new command and it is also more suitable. In comparison with the previous temporary command, this command is now fit to remain permanent and everlasting, till eternity.

Allah alone knows everything. The example of the verses of Allah is like that of a patient who is given medicine drop by drop until he is cured. Now, instead of medicine, he is given ordinary food so that he may live an ordinary life.

But the polytheists of Makkah were not aware of this wisdom, so they could not understand why one verse was coming after another, and why laws were changing even during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ). They attributed this to the idea that the Prophet (ﷺ) was, God forbid, fabricating verses on his own, although they knew that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is truthful and trustworthy and never tells a lie, let alone that he would lie about Allah.

﴿بَلْ أَكْثَرُهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (16:101) "Rather, most of them do not know."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verse 102:

﴿Say: It has been sent down by the Holy Spirit (Jibril) from your Lord, in truth, gradually.﴾ (16:102 in the Urdu citation's numbering: 61:201) So there is no room left for the possibility of fabrication. It was brought by the Holy Spirit, it was brought from Allah, and its teachings are based on truth. There is not even a trace of falsehood in them. It came for this purpose: ﴿to strengthen those who believe﴾ (61:201), so that their hearts become attached to Allah and they recognize that these teachings are from Allah. They should hold firmly to the truth and be satisfied with its veracity, so that ﴿it may be a guidance and good news for those who submit﴾ (61:201), showing them the straight path in the affairs of life and giving them the glad tidings of happiness and success. This good news concerns, in particular, victory and establishment in the land.

﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him." The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ (16:103)

Their second fabrication was that perhaps some man was teaching the Qur'an to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They even mentioned his name. However, the reports about him differ. They were pointing to a foreign slave who in fact belonged to some of the clans of Quraysh, and who used to trade near the Halafa'. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to sit with him. This man was a foreigner and did not know the Arabic language; he had only a basic, necessary familiarity with Arabic.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrates: It has reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to sit near a Christian slave in Marwah, whose name was Jabr. He belonged to the Banu al-Hadrami branch. So this verse was revealed concerning him:

﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him." The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ (16:103)

Abdullah ibn Kathir has said, and transmitted from Ikrimah and Qatadah, that his name was Bu'aysh. Ibn Kathir has narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach a slave. This man was in Makkah and his name was Balam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to go to him. The polytheists knew that the Prophet (ﷺ) came and went to him, so they made this accusation, that Balam was teaching him these teachings.

Whatever the name may be, the refutation that Allah the Exalted has given of this accusation is simple and unanswerable. And is it not evident to you that the man you speak of has a foreign tongue, whereas the Qur'an is in clear Arabic?

The accusation those people levelled against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cannot be called a serious accusation; rather, it was a scheme of false propaganda on their part. For they knew well the literary and doctrinal worth of the Qur'an and its inimitability. It was simply impossible for any foreigner to teach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) such speech. If a foreigner could produce this kind of speech, why would he not present it as his own words?

Today, when humanity has advanced greatly, and the art of composition and writing has progressed far because of human ability, and the most modern methods of legislation and administration have come into being, no one with even ordinary knowledge, and no one familiar with social and legal systems, can imagine that this book could be the composition of a single human being.

The materialists and atheists of Russia also hold the view that this Qur'an cannot be the composition of one person. They say it is the work of a whole group, and that some of its parts could not even have been composed in the Arabian Peninsula; some of its parts are certainly said to have been brought in from outside. They compiled these writings in 1945 as a result of the conference they convened to criticise the Qur'an.

The Russians put forward this proposal because they held that a single person could not possess such ability as to compose such a book, nor could it be the work of any one nation. But the Russians did not have the grace to accept the simple and plain truth that this book cannot be a human composition, and therefore it is the revelation of the Lord of the Worlds. However, since they were materialists and atheists, and denied the existence of God, the Messengers and prophethood itself, they did not accept this truth.

If the thinking of the orientalists of the twentieth century is that the Qur'an cannot be the composition of a single human being, then how could it be the composition of a foreign slave of the Arabian Peninsula?

The Qur'an states the reason for their statements: "Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah – Allah does not guide them, and for them is a painful punishment" (16:104). "Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah does not guide them to the right word, and for such people there is a painful punishment."

These people who do not believe in the signs of Allah – Allah has not granted them the ability to form a correct opinion about this Book. Nor can they find their way to the true reality, because they have decided that they will disbelieve, turn away, and never accept it. Therefore: "for them is a painful punishment" (16:104).

Here it is now being shown how the trustworthy Messenger could fabricate lies against Allah. Such an act is committed only by wicked people who keep on fabricating falsehoods.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verse 105:

"Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies, and it is they who are the liars." (61: 501) "(It is not the Prophet who invents falsehoods); rather, it is those who are fabricating lies who do not believe in the signs of Allah. It is they who are truly liars."

Lying is such a despicable sin that no believer can ever tell a lie. In a hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) clearly stated that a Muslim cannot tell a lie, although a Muslim may commit other sins.

Now, from here onward, the rulings concerning those who choose disbelief after faith are being explained.

The early period in Makkah saw the Muslims subjected to such persecution and such hardships that bearing them was possible only for a person who had intended martyrdom, who had given the Hereafter precedence over the worldly life, and who was prepared to face the most severe torment rather than return to disbelief after Islam.

Here it is explained that, after having believed, adopting disbelief is a grave crime. For to renounce faith after having known it and tasted it, and to choose disbelief over the Hereafter, is a very great crime. Such people will incur the wrath of Allah, they will deserve a great punishment, and they will be deprived of guidance forever and ever. Such people are sunk in heedlessness. Seals are set upon their hearts, their ears and their eyes, and in the Hereafter these people will suffer a very great loss. The reason is that no movement can bargain concerning its ideology, and no consideration of gain or loss is given regarding the ideology and the call. When a person believes and accepts the Islamic way of life, then none of the influences of this earth and this world should affect that person, because the earth has its own reckoning and value, and ideologies have their own worth. An ideology is not a jest; there can be no bargaining over ideologies, because ideologies stand at a level above bargaining. This is precisely why such severity has been applied to the punishment for this act. There is one exception to this severe ruling: that a person has been compelled to declare disbelief while his heart remains content in faith. That is, a person may utter a declaration of disbelief in a state where he faces the threat of death, while his heart is at rest in faith and certainty.

It is related in the narrations that this verse was revealed concerning Ammar ibn Yasir.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Yasir that the polytheists seized Ammar ibn Yasir and inflicted severe pain upon him. They subjected him to such great torment that he came close to saying what they wished. He complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he had said these things because of the torment. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "My heart is content in faith." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If they subject you to such torment again, then say those words again." Thus, permission and dispensation were granted to utter words of disbelief in such difficult circumstances.

Some Muslims also passed away who preferred death over uttering a word of disbelief merely with the tongue. Sumayyah bint Khayyat (the mother of Ammar ibn Yasir) attained this lofty station of resolve; a spear was thrust into her private parts, and she was martyred. Likewise Abu Yasir also attained this station. Both were martyred, but neither uttered a word of disbelief.

And what was not done to Bilal (may Allah be pleased with him)? A huge stone would be placed upon his chest in the scorching heat, and he would be told to say the words of polytheism. He would refuse and say "Ahad, Ahad" (One, One), and he would say: "If I knew of any harsher word than this, I would say that too."

The same was the condition of Habib ibn Zayd al-Ansari. Musaylimah the Liar said to him: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah?" He would say, "Yes." Then he said: "Do you testify that I am a messenger?" He would reply: "I am not hearing." So he kept cutting off his limbs, until he was martyred in that state.

Ibn Asakir, in the biography of Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi, has written that he was a Companion. The Romans captured him and presented him before their king. The king said to him: "Become a Christian, and I will share my authority with you and give you my daughter in marriage." He said: "Even if you were to give me your entire kingdom and the rule of all the Arabs, in exchange for my abandoning the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) even for the blink of an eye, I would not do it." The king said: "Then I will kill you." He said: "You have the authority; do whatever you wish." It is said that he gave an order and he was crucified. Then he ordered the archers to shoot arrows near his feet and hands. So they kept shooting, and the king kept presenting the religion of Christianity to him, but he refused. After that, he ordered that he be taken down from the cross. Then a cauldron of copper (or a pot of oil) was brought and heated. Afterwards a Muslim captive was brought and thrown into it, and in a moment he became shining bones. Then he again presented his religion to him, and he refused. Now the king ordered that he too be thrown into it. He was placed upon an iron wheel so that he could be thrown in. At that moment he wept. The king then felt a greed that perhaps he would now agree, and so he called him. He said: "I wept because my life is one, and it is about to be put into this cauldron and finished. But my wish is that there were as many lives as there are hairs on my body, and that they were all sacrificed in the way of Allah."

In another narration, it is stated that he imprisoned him and withheld food. This restriction continued for a period. Then they sent him wine and pork, and he did not touch them. So he was summoned and asked why he had not touched them. He said: "These things are lawful for me at this time, but I do not wish to please you." Then the king said: "Come, kiss my head, and I will set you free." He said: "Will you release all the Muslim prisoners along with me?" The king said: "Yes." So he kissed his head, and he released all the prisoners who were with him. When he returned, Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It is the right of every Muslim to kiss the head of Abdullah ibn Hudhafah, and I will begin it." He rose and kissed his head. May Allah be pleased with both of them.

Lesson 421: An Overview

It has already been noted that Allah, in this Surah, explains the Islamic creed of Tawhid through two examples. Here an example is given concerning the people of Makkah, the idolaters of Quraysh and the conditions of Makkah. Allah had showered His bounties upon the people of Makkah, but they did not give thanks for His blessings. Through this example, Allah wishes to warn the people of Makkah about the end that awaits them in the veils of the future.

The blessings mentioned in this example are abundant provision and the blessing of peace and tranquility that existed in Makkah. In this connection, they are also presented with the fact that, because of idol worship, they have unnecessarily forbidden to themselves certain good and lawful things, although Allah has declared these things lawful. Allah has explained the forbidden things, and these things are not among them. This too is, in a sense, ingratitude for the blessings of Allah. As a result of such ingratitude, a painful punishment may also descend upon you, and this is a very great fabrication against Allah; Allah has issued no command for the prohibition of these things.

Then, regarding the impure things that were forbidden to the Muslims, mention is also made of those things that were forbidden to the Jews. These things were forbidden to them as punishments for certain crimes. Moreover, they were forbidden as a punishment for some of their injustices. They were not forbidden from the era of Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who was a community in himself, devoted and upright (hanif), who did not associate partners with Allah, and to whom Allah had given guidance. He was chosen and was upon the Straight Path. These good things were lawful for him and for his progeny as well. Until, in later periods, they were forbidden to the Children of Israel as a punishment, and if they did not repent of these ignorant practices, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

After this, as a continuation of the religion of Ibrahim, the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) came, and in it all the good things that were lawful in the religion of Ibrahim were made lawful again. Similarly, the hunting that had been prohibited for the Jews on the Sabbath day was also made lawful, because the Jews had made the observance of the Sabbath questionable. Some people desisted, and some broke the observance of the Sabbath. Therefore Allah made those people questionable as well. Some people desisted and some broke the observance of the Sabbath. Therefore Allah distorted the faces of those people and degraded them from the rank of humanity.

In this context, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is commanded to call to the way of Allah with wisdom and fine admonition, and to debate with them in the most graceful manner. If you are wronged, then retaliation should be just in its manner; in no case should limits be exceeded. If the opponent is forgiven and patience is exercised, that is best of all. After this, know that the good end belongs only to the God-fearing and the doers of good, because Allah is with those who have taqwa and those who do ihsan. Allah helps them, watches over them, and continues to guide them to the path of righteousness and success.

This example applies fully to Makkah. Allah established the House of Allah (Bayt Allah) in that town, then made it a sanctuary (Balad Haram) by bringing it into motion. Whoever enters it becomes safe and secure. No one is permitted to raise a hand against anyone within it, even if that person is a murderer. As long as he remains within the House of Allah, no one dares to raise a hand against him. The condition of the Arabian Peninsula was that there was no security in the areas around Makkah, and people were snatched away. But the people of Makkah lived in peace at all times and passed their lives in complete tranquility. Moreover, their provisions kept arriving from every direction, with the pilgrims and with peaceful trade caravans, although they dwelt in a valley without cultivation (ghayr dhi zar'). Despite this, the fruit of every thing and every kind of produce reached them. Thus they enjoyed security and lived a life of prosperity. This had been their condition since the time Hadrat Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam) prayed for them.

Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came, and these people knew him well. They called him Al-Sadiq (the Truthful) and Al-Amin (the Trustworthy). They found no weakness in him. Then Allah bestowed prophethood upon him (ﷺ) so that he (ﷺ) might reform them and the whole universe spread around them. The religion of the Messenger (ﷺ) is also the religion of Ibrahim, who built the House of Allah. In the shelter of its mercy these people live a life of security and tranquility, and they are living a life of great prosperity and affluence. Yet these people deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), make all kinds of accusations against him (ﷺ), and inflict all kinds of hardships and oppression upon him (ﷺ) and upon his followers.

This is the example of a town which Allah gives for the people of Makkah, and it fully fits their own circumstances. Its outcome lies in their own situation, just as Allah gave the example of the village whose inhabitants were content and at peace, and provisions were arriving for them in abundance from every direction. But they were ungrateful for the blessings of Allah and denied the Messenger of Allah. Then what happened?

﴿So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear, because of what they used to do﴾ (16:112). "Then Allah made the inhabitants taste the consequences of their deeds, so that hunger and fear would be their garment." Other punishments also came upon them, because they were wrongdoers. Here Allah personifies fear and hunger as a garment. It is as though they remain in that state at all times, and hunger and destitution are their garment, which they do not wear but taste, because merely wearing a garment is less effective than tasting it. The manner of expression is such that both the faculty of taste and the faculty of touch work together, and thus the sense of hunger and fear is doubled and the matter settles firmly in the soul. This very vivid manner of expression has been adopted so that they may think carefully about the outcome that awaits them.

In this example, on one side, the notion of Allah's blessings and provision is given, and on the other side, the idea of their deprivation is given. In keeping with this, it is said here that they should eat of the good things (tayyibat) which Allah has made lawful for them, and give thanks to Allah. Worship and obey Allah alone. Walk straight on the path of faith and beware of polytheism, because of which their so-called gods have declared some good things unlawfully forbidden to them.

Commentary: Allah defines the boundaries of what is forbidden (muharramat). The forbidden things are enumerated, so that it is clear that nothing other than these is forbidden. In this enumeration are not included those things which they (the people) have made forbidden upon themselves on their own accord. For example, bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah and ham.

These things have been made unlawful for various reasons: either because they cause physical harm, or sensory harm, such as carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine; or because they cause psychological and ideological harm, such as animals slaughtered in the name of other than Allah.

Verse: ﴿But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (521)

Translation: "However, whoever is compelled by hunger and is driven to desperation, and eats these things without desiring to disobey the law of Allah or without transgressing the limit of necessity, then surely Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

This is because the religion of Islam is an easy religion, and in it there is no unnecessary hardship upon anyone. A person who fears death, or fears a severe illness from hunger, or fears severe thirst, may use these things to the extent of need. There are jurisprudential differences on this matter, which we have mentioned earlier. The meaning of "ghayr baghin" (neither desiring) is that he is not one who breaks the principle of prohibition, and the meaning of "ghayr 'adin" (nor exceeding the limit) is that he does not go beyond the measure of necessity, because permission has been granted only to the extent of need.

These are the limits of the lawful and the unlawful which Allah has set regarding foodstuffs. Therefore, do not transgress these limits of lawful and unlawful as a result of idolatrous illusions, lest you tell lies by declaring the things Allah has made lawful to be unlawful and saying that this is the command of Allah, because the determination of the limits of lawful and unlawful belongs solely to the authority of Allah. It relates to legislation, and the authority of legislation belongs only to Allah. Whoever legislates without the permission of Allah and without evidence from the Qur'an and Sunnah, and considers himself entitled to it, is a liar, and liars can never succeed with Allah.

"As for what your tongues falsely describe, saying, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful,' do not say so. That would be a fabrication against Allah." Such people will certainly enjoy some comforts during the brief life of this world, but in the Hereafter there is a punishment for them, and these people will be in severe loss.

Despite these verses, some people in Islamic countries carry out legislative work, and make laws that are in clear contradiction to the Qur'an and Sunnah, and yet they hope that they will be successful in this world and the Hereafter; rather, they deserve a great punishment.

The Qur'an presents Ibrahim (peace be upon him) as a model of guidance, an embodiment of turning back to Allah (inabah), a figure of patience and gratitude, and one who was obedient and devoted in worship. Here it is said that he was "ummah" (a community), meaning that the obedience, turning to Allah, and gratitude and blessing that were in him were equal to those of an entire community. Or its meaning would be that he was an "imam" (leader) of guidance... Both meanings have been reported from the exegetes (mufassirin), and the two meanings are close to each other. This is because whoever leads others to the path of guidance is the leader of the community, and such an imam will also receive the reward of all those whom he showed the path of guidance. Thus this guide himself becomes a community; he does not remain a single individual.

"Hanifan" (61:120) means one who turns towards the truth, who has an inward inclination towards what is right.

"Wa lam yaku min al-mushrikin" (61:120): "and he was not among the polytheists." Therefore, polytheists have no right to display their connection to him, nor to seek blessing through him.

Up to this point the discussion has concerned the distinction between the new religion, pure monotheistic belief, the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham) and the connection between his monotheism and these, and the deviant beliefs of the polytheists and the Jews. This was also one of the important aims of the Qur'an. Now, at the end, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is admonished to continue advancing on the path of his Lord and to propagate his call with the best admonition, wisdom and moderation. If it becomes necessary to debate with opponents, it should be conducted in the most excellent manner. Yes, if opponents assault the Islamic movement, do not exceed limits in retaliation, and keep your reciprocal action limited to the extent of retribution. Yes, if you overlook some of the opponents' pardonable actions, that is much better. Be assured that the good end belongs surely to those who fear Allah. Do not be distressed on account of these people. If they do not accept, and if they devise plots against you and against the Muslims, then do not care. Allah is with you.

This is the method of the Islamic call (da'wah), and these are the principles and rules for the work of the Islamic movement. This method was laid down for the Prophet ﷺ himself. Moreover, it is the code of conduct and the method of da'wah for all the callers to truth who come after him ﷺ.

First of all, this da'wah is a call to Allah. The call is to the way of Allah and to the system of Allah, not to any personality or to any nation. In this, the role of the caller is only that he is performing his duty. Therefore, calling to the faith is not a favour on his part, so that he should go about boasting of it. It is neither a favour upon the Islamic da'wah nor a favour upon those who become followers of the caller. Therefore, its reward is also upon Allah.

The da'wah should continue with wisdom (hikmah) and good planning. The circumstances and conditions of the listener should be kept in view in it, and it should be determined how much da'wah should be given to the listener at one time. It should not be that so many commands and prohibitions are recited to people in a short time, while they are not mentally prepared for them. In that case they will consider it a burden, an unbearable burden. The method of da'wah should be appropriate, should accord with circumstances and conditions, and should keep changing accordingly. The caller should not become harsh in excitement, nor should he create more enthusiasm and zeal than wisdom allows. He should act with moderation in every matter.

Its manner of admonition should be gentle and extremely attractive. The speech should be in such a manner that it sits in the heart and mind. Do not adopt only the style of abuse and of shaming people. Also, the caller should not expose the mistakes that someone commits out of ignorance and folly. Sometimes such mistakes occur with good intention. Through gentleness in admonition, sometimes even very rebellious people and those fallen from morality attain guidance. A diamond's heart can be cut by a petal of a flower, but scolding, reproach, and cursing and blaming sometimes have a reverse effect.

If an occasion of debate arises with them, it too should be conducted in the best manner. It would not be appropriate for the caller to attack the opponent and humiliate him, or to enumerate his faults. In the style of debate in da'wah, the listener should be convinced that the one calling does not seek mere domination and superiority in speech, but that the caller only wishes to make a truth clear to the mind. Every human being has some measure of the tendency to obstinacy, and every person has self-respect. He wants to defend his opinion until the end, so that he is protected from every humiliation and defeat. Belief and ideology are, in essence, opinion, and people raise the value of their opinion so much that if someone is asked to change his opinion, they think that their prestige, their dignity, and their personality will be diminished. If the caller conducts debate and dialogue in a good manner, then the personal feelings of a person will not be hurt by it, and the listener will understand that his self-respect, his personality, and his honour and dignity are preserved, and that the caller only wishes to convey the message, and is calling him to a good path purely for the sake of Allah. He has no personal aim attached to this task; he does not desire his own victory or the defeat of the listener.

In order to reduce the excessive zeal and passion of the caller, the Qur'anic text points to this: in truth, Allah is the most knowing; He alone knows who has strayed and who is about to be guided. Therefore, there is no need for great excitement and contention within debate and discussion. Rather, the call should be given in a refined manner, and after that its results should be left to Allah.

As long as the activity in the Islamic da'wah is confined to verbal invitation and debate with argument, this is the Islamic code of conduct for da'wah. But if the opponent resorts to physical aggression, then this policy will no longer apply, because physical aggression is a tangible and material act. To uphold the honour of truth and to maintain the station of truth, it is necessary that aggression from falsehood be given an appropriate response. It should not be that falsehood fully dominates the atmosphere. Yet the response to the aggression of falsehood should also remain within limits and bounds. It should not be that the opponent is humiliated and given an exemplary punishment, because Islam is a just religion. It greatly loves peace and safety. Islam only seeks the defence of its own self and of the people of Islam. It in no way accepts oppression and physical aggression.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 16, verses 126–127:

﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the same as that with which you were afflicted﴾ (16:126). "If you take revenge, then take only as much as you were wronged." This is not something outside the method of the Islamic call (da'wah); rather, it is within it. Defending the Islamic call and adopting a balanced attitude in this matter will be a cause of the dignity and honour of the Islamic movement. In people's hearts, it will not be a worthless call. A call that lacks dignity is never accepted by people; nor do people believe that it is the true religion. Moreover, it is not God's intention to leave the Islamic call so humiliated and helpless that it cannot defend its own honour and dignity. Therefore, the people of faith, as long as they are callers to the religion of God, cannot bear humiliation at all. Furthermore, the duty of the caller is to be a trustee of truth on this earth. It is for him to establish justice and equity among people, and it is he who must lead humanity towards the right path. They cannot do this if they are punished and are unable to take revenge, and are unable to properly rebuke the aggressor.

In this matter, the principle of a suitable response and rebuke will be the principle of qisas (retribution). The real intention of the Qur'an is that a person should adopt forgiveness and pardon. But forgiveness and pardon occur when a person has the power to take revenge and retaliate, and in such circumstances forgiveness and pardon have a very good effect, and the call benefits greatly. If some individuals are attacked but the call benefits, then aggression against individuals has no significance. But if forgiveness would result in the insult of the call to God (da'wah ila Allah) and its dignity would be harmed, then in that case the principle of qisas is better. Since by patience and forbearance the caller learns to control his feelings and his desire for revenge, the Qur'an therefore links this act and its reward to God and the Hereafter.

﴿And if you endure patiently, it is certainly better for the patient﴾ (16:126). ﴿And be patient; and your patience is not except through God﴾ (16:127). "But if you are patient, it is surely better for those who are patient. And be patient; your patience is only for God." It is God who grants the ability to be patient and to control oneself, and He is the helper of a person in this; and it is this sense of devotion to God that inclines a person towards patience rather than personal revenge, retribution and retaliation.

The Qur'an, in the manner of advice to the Prophet ﷺ, is establishing this principle, and for every caller to religion, including you, this is the code of conduct: that if people do not come onto the path of guidance, he should not be distressed. His duty is only what he is performing. Guidance and misguidance are in the hand of God. Guidance and misguidance accord with the Sunnah of God, and the Sunnah of God is the capacity which God has placed within human souls for guidance and misguidance. Also, the caller should not become dejected because of the deceit of opponents, for he is a caller; God is his protector. It is He who will respond to the deceit and intrigues of the opponents. God does not hand over a caller to his opponents, provided he is sincere in the call, is working for God, and has no personal interest in view.

That he is being tormented is a test of his patience. The delay in the arrival of God's help is because his trust and certainty in God are being tested; but the good outcome is certain, and victory is about to embrace his feet.

Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him (taqwa) and those who do good (ihsan).

Whoever has Allah with him has nothing to fear. Let whoever wishes plot against him and devise schemes against him; Allah, in any case, does not leave His righteous servants alone.

This is the code of conduct (dustur al-amal) of the Islamic call (da'wah), which Allah Himself, the Exalted, has laid down. If the caller (da'i) follows it, success is certain. This is the word of Allah, and who can speak more truly than Allah?
